title: Repeated transformer trips during monsoon load peaks
problem: A 220/33kV transformer kept tripping on differential protection during the monsoon evening load peak, roughly twice a week.
context: Substation commissioned in 2011, feeding a semi-urban distribution network. The trips only happened after heavy rain and only during the 18:00 to 21:00 load block.
decision: We stopped treating it as a transformer fault and instead instrumented the CT secondary circuits in the marshalling kiosk before touching the transformer itself.
reasoning: A genuine internal transformer fault does not politely wait for rain. The correlation with weather pointed at insulation or wiring in an enclosure, not at the winding. Differential protection only needs one CT circuit to misbehave to produce a false operation.
mistake: For the first three weeks the team assumed the transformer winding was failing and scheduled an expensive oil and DGA test cycle.
root_cause: Water ingress through a cracked cable gland in the marshalling box was intermittently shorting one CT secondary, unbalancing the differential relay.
outcome: Replacing the gland and re-sealing the kiosk removed the trips completely. No transformer work was needed and the planned outage was cancelled.
lesson: When a protection trip correlates with weather or time of day, suspect the secondary wiring and enclosures before suspecting the primary plant.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish someone had told me to always plot trip timestamps against weather and load curves on day one. That single graph would have saved three weeks.

title: Earthing grid that passed on paper and failed in the field
problem: Touch potential measured at a new switchyard was far above the design value even though the earthing grid drawing was fully compliant.
context: Rocky terrain site. The soil resistivity survey had been done in a single season during a dry month.
decision: We re-ran the soil resistivity survey at multiple points and depths instead of trusting the single original survey, then added supplementary rods and a buried conductor ring.
reasoning: Grid design is only as good as the resistivity input. A single measurement point on rocky ground can under-report resistivity by a large factor, and every downstream calculation inherits that error.
mistake: We accepted a single-point, single-season soil resistivity report as the design basis for the whole grid.
root_cause: Actual soil resistivity was around three times the surveyed value because the original measurement was taken in one unrepresentative low-resistivity pocket.
outcome: After the supplementary electrodes were installed, measured touch and step potentials came within limits and the switchyard was energised two months late.
lesson: Verify the input data of a design, not just the arithmetic of the design. A compliant calculation on wrong inputs is still an unsafe installation.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to treat any single-point survey as a hypothesis rather than as data.

title: Payment API latency spike traced to connection pool exhaustion
problem: The payment API p99 latency jumped from 180ms to over 9 seconds during a sale event, while CPU and memory looked completely healthy.
context: Microservice on Kubernetes talking to a primary relational database, traffic roughly four times a normal weekday peak.
decision: We looked at connection pool saturation and database wait events first, rather than scaling out more application pods.
reasoning: Healthy CPU with terrible latency almost always means the service is waiting on something, not computing. Adding pods when the bottleneck is a shared downstream resource makes contention worse, not better.
mistake: The first reflex from the on-call team was to double the replica count, which briefly made latency worse.
root_cause: Each pod held a fixed pool of 20 connections. Scaling pods multiplied total connections past the database max_connections limit, so new connections queued and then timed out.
outcome: Reducing per-pod pool size and putting a connection proxy in front of the database brought p99 back under 300ms within the same event.
lesson: Horizontal scaling multiplies your pressure on shared downstream resources. Always ask what the bottleneck actually is before adding instances.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had understood earlier that connection limits are a shared global budget, not a per-service setting.

title: A retry storm turned a small outage into a long one
problem: A 40 second database failover became a 50 minute customer-facing outage across several unrelated services.
context: Service mesh with default retry settings, roughly a dozen services in the call chain during checkout.
decision: We disabled retries at intermediate hops and kept them only at the edge, and added jittered exponential backoff with a retry budget.
reasoning: Retries at every layer multiply. Three hops each retrying three times is twenty-seven requests for one user action. When the dependency is already struggling, that traffic amplification prevents it from ever recovering.
mistake: We had enabled generous retries independently in each service because each team thought it was making their own service more resilient.
root_cause: Multiplicative retry amplification kept the recovering database saturated long after the failover itself had completed.
outcome: In the next planned failover test the same 40 second event produced only a 55 second degradation with no customer impact.
lesson: Resilience decisions taken independently in each service can add up to a system-wide fragility. Retries need a global budget.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to draw the full call graph and multiply the retry counts before approving any retry policy.

title: Differential settlement under a warehouse slab
problem: A newly built warehouse slab developed visible cracking and a 40mm level difference across expansion joints within eight months.
context: Reclaimed coastal land, single storey structure with heavy racking loads concentrated along one wall.
decision: We commissioned additional boreholes along the settled edge rather than repairing the visible cracks, and then designed a targeted underpinning scheme.
reasoning: Cracking is a symptom. Repairing a symptom on a settling foundation just produces new cracks next season. The pattern of settlement follows the ground, so the ground had to be characterised first.
mistake: The original site investigation used boreholes spaced too widely and missed a compressible clay lens under one corner of the footprint.
root_cause: A soft clay layer of variable thickness under part of the footprint consolidated under the concentrated racking load.
outcome: Targeted underpinning plus a redistribution of the racking layout stabilised the slab. Movement monitoring showed less than 3mm over the following two years.
lesson: Borehole spacing must reflect geological variability, not just the convenience of the survey budget. On reclaimed land, assume variability until proven otherwise.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to push back harder on a cheap site investigation. The saving was tiny compared with the remediation cost.

title: Chloride attack on coastal reinforced concrete
problem: Reinforcement corrosion and spalling appeared on a coastal structure roughly twelve years into a design life of fifty years.
context: Splash zone elements, marine exposure, concrete specified to the general durability clause rather than to a marine-specific mix design.
decision: We moved from patch repair to cathodic protection for the splash zone elements after chloride profiling showed contamination well past the bar depth.
reasoning: Patch repair on chloride-contaminated concrete often accelerates corrosion in the adjacent parent concrete, because the repaired patch becomes a cathode. Chloride profiles, not visual damage extent, decide the right strategy.
mistake: The first two repair campaigns were cosmetic patch repairs done without any chloride profiling.
root_cause: Cover depth and mix permeability were specified for a general environment, so chloride ingress reached the reinforcement far faster than the design assumed.
outcome: Cathodic protection halted active corrosion. Monitoring over four years showed stable potentials and no new spalling.
lesson: In marine exposure, cover and permeability matter more than concrete strength grade. Measure chlorides before choosing a repair strategy.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known how badly a well-intentioned patch repair can make the neighbouring concrete worse.

title: Gearbox failures caused by a misread vibration signature
problem: A critical gearbox failed twice in fourteen months despite a full condition monitoring programme being in place.
context: Continuous process line, weekly vibration route measurements, alarms configured on overall RMS velocity only.
decision: We added spectrum and envelope analysis at gear mesh frequency and sidebands instead of relying on overall vibration levels.
reasoning: Overall RMS is dominated by low-frequency energy such as unbalance and misalignment. Early gear tooth damage shows up as small sidebands around mesh frequency, which barely moves the overall number until failure is close.
mistake: We trusted a single overall vibration number as the health indicator for a complex multi-stage gearbox.
root_cause: Gear tooth spalling progressed for months while the overall RMS reading stayed inside the green band, so no alarm ever fired.
outcome: The revised programme detected an early defect on a sister gearbox nine weeks before it would have failed, and the repair was done in a planned shutdown.
lesson: Choose the measurement that matches the failure mode. A monitoring programme that cannot see the failure mode is not monitoring, it is paperwork.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known that a green dashboard often means the wrong thing is being measured rather than that the machine is healthy.

title: Pump cavitation blamed on the pump for two years
problem: A feed pump eroded its impeller repeatedly, with each replacement lasting only around seven months.
context: Suction taken from an open tank through a long suction line with a strainer, plant throughput increased in 2018 without a hydraulic review.
decision: We calculated available NPSH at the new flow rate rather than ordering another impeller in a harder material.
reasoning: Repeated identical erosion is a system problem, not a component problem. Changing the component only changes how long the system takes to destroy it.
mistake: Two full years of maintenance budget went into replacing impellers and upgrading materials without anyone recalculating the suction hydraulics.
root_cause: The throughput increase pushed available NPSH below required NPSH at the higher flow, so the pump cavitated during normal operation.
outcome: Raising the tank level set point and cleaning up the suction line restored the NPSH margin. The next impeller ran for over three years.
lesson: When a component fails the same way repeatedly, stop replacing it and go re-derive the operating conditions it now actually lives in.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to treat every capacity increase as a trigger to recheck every hydraulic assumption downstream and upstream.

title: Random device resets that only happened in the field
problem: A battery powered device reset randomly at customer sites but never once in three months of lab testing.
context: Portable medical device, mains charger used in the field, lab bench used a linear regulated supply.
decision: We reproduced the field environment on the bench, including the actual switching charger and a long charging cable, instead of adding more firmware watchdogs.
reasoning: A defect that never reproduces in the lab usually means the lab is not the real environment. The difference between lab and field is the clue, so we listed every difference and tested them one at a time.
mistake: The first response was to add watchdog timers and reset counters in firmware, which hid the symptom and delayed the real diagnosis by two months.
root_cause: Conducted noise from the customer's switching charger coupled into the reset line, which had no filtering capacitor near the microcontroller.
outcome: Adding a 100nF capacitor and a series resistor on the reset line eliminated the resets. Field returns for this fault dropped to zero over the next year.
lesson: If a bug will not reproduce, fix the test environment before fixing the product. Firmware workarounds on hardware noise problems only hide the evidence.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to write down every difference between the bench and the field on day one instead of trusting the bench.

title: Battery life collapsed because of a single sleep-mode pin
problem: A device specified for 30 days of battery life was returning from the field flat after about 4 days.
context: Low power firmware with the microcontroller correctly entering deep sleep, verified by firmware logs.
decision: We measured actual sleep current with a current probe on the real assembled unit rather than trusting the firmware sleep logs.
reasoning: Firmware can only report what it did, not what the board actually drew. Anything outside the microcontroller, such as a floating pin or an external sensor, is invisible to firmware logs.
mistake: We assumed the sleep problem had to be in the firmware because the firmware was the part we could see and change quickly.
root_cause: One GPIO driving a sensor enable line was left floating in sleep, keeping an external sensor partially powered and drawing about 2mA continuously.
outcome: Explicitly driving that pin low in the sleep routine brought sleep current from 2.1mA to 12uA and the device met the 30 day target.
lesson: Measure the physical quantity you are actually promising. Logs describe intent, instruments describe reality.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known that every unconfigured GPIO is a potential leak path, and to audit all of them before the first battery test.

title: Checkout slowed to a crawl after a harmless-looking index change
problem: Checkout p95 latency went from 240ms to 4.5s the morning after a routine schema migration, with no error rate increase.
context: Order service on a single primary database. The migration added one column and dropped an index nobody thought was used.
decision: We read the query plans for the three slowest endpoints before rolling anything back.
reasoning: A rollback would have restored service but destroyed the evidence. Plans show exactly which access path changed, and that is the only way to know whether the migration or the traffic pattern was responsible.
mistake: The dropped index was judged unused from a query-name search rather than from actual database statistics.
root_cause: A composite index was serving a query the search missed, so the planner fell back to a sequential scan on a 40 million row table.
outcome: Recreating the index concurrently brought p95 back to 250ms within twenty minutes, with no rollback needed.
lesson: Prove an index is unused from database usage statistics, not from reading application code. The code does not know what the planner chose.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to capture query plans before every migration, so the comparison is instant instead of archaeological.

title: A cache that made the outage worse when it expired
problem: Every Monday at 09:00 the product service spiked to 100% CPU for about ninety seconds and shed traffic.
context: Catalogue data cached with a fixed 24 hour TTL, set at deploy time, so every key expired at the same instant.
decision: We added jitter to the TTL and a stale-while-revalidate window instead of increasing the cache size.
reasoning: The spike was periodic and identical each week, which points at synchronised expiry rather than load. A bigger cache would still empty all at once.
mistake: We treated a thundering herd as a capacity problem and had already scaled the service twice.
root_cause: All cache keys were written in the same deploy window with an identical TTL, so they expired simultaneously and every request went to the database at once.
outcome: Randomising the TTL over a two hour window removed the spike completely, and we scaled the service back down.
lesson: Anything that expires on a fixed schedule will eventually expire all at once. Spread expiry deliberately.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known that a perfectly regular spike is almost never a capacity problem.

title: An access review that found permissions nobody had ever removed
problem: A quarterly access review found 60 accounts with production database write access, against an engineering team of 24.
context: Permissions were granted individually during incidents and never tied to a role or an expiry.
decision: We moved to time-bound break-glass access rather than trying to audit the existing grants one by one.
reasoning: Auditing a list that grows faster than you can review it is a losing game. Making access expire by default turns a permanent audit problem into a temporary one.
mistake: For three years access was granted permanently during incidents because it was faster in the moment, with no follow-up.
root_cause: There was no expiry mechanism, so every emergency grant became permanent by default.
outcome: Standing write access dropped to four accounts. Break-glass grants now expire after four hours and are logged.
lesson: Access granted under pressure must expire on its own. Anything relying on someone remembering to revoke it will accumulate.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to make the temporary path the easy path from the start.

title: A dependency vulnerability that was not actually reachable
problem: A critical CVE in a parsing library triggered an emergency patch cycle across eleven services.
context: Automated scanning flagged the library by version, with no analysis of whether the vulnerable code path was used.
decision: We checked call reachability for each service before scheduling emergency work.
reasoning: Severity scores describe the worst case for anyone using the library. What matters is whether your code can reach the vulnerable function with attacker-controlled input.
mistake: The first response was to schedule out-of-hours patching for all eleven services at once.
root_cause: Only two services parsed untrusted input with that library. The other nine used a different entry point that never reached the vulnerable code.
outcome: Two services were patched urgently, nine went into the normal cycle. No emergency weekend work was needed.
lesson: A CVE score is not a risk assessment for your system. Reachability decides urgency.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to keep a dependency-to-entry-point map, so reachability takes minutes rather than days.

title: A health check that reported healthy while the service was useless
problem: A service kept serving traffic and passing health checks for forty minutes while every request it made downstream failed.
context: The readiness probe returned 200 from a handler that did nothing but confirm the process was alive.
decision: We changed the probe to verify the service's critical dependency, with a short timeout and a cached result.
reasoning: A health check that cannot fail is decoration. It should assert the thing that makes the service useful, not the thing that is trivially true.
mistake: We assumed a passing probe meant a working service, so the incident was investigated everywhere except the failing service.
root_cause: The probe never touched the database connection, so a pool that had lost all its connections still reported ready.
outcome: In the next similar failure the pod was removed from rotation in eleven seconds instead of forty minutes.
lesson: Make health checks assert something that can actually break. A probe that only proves the process started tells you nothing.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to test health checks by deliberately breaking the dependency and watching what the probe says.

title: A deploy pipeline that was green while shipping nothing
problem: A bug fix was reported as deployed for six days but the fix was never actually running in production.
context: Pipeline with a build stage, a test stage and a deploy stage, each reporting its own status.
decision: We added a post-deploy verification step that queries the running service for its build identifier.
reasoning: A pipeline reports that its steps ran, not that the system changed. The only trustworthy signal comes from the running system itself.
mistake: We trusted a green pipeline as proof of deployment for years without ever verifying against the running service.
root_cause: The deploy step pushed to a registry tag that the cluster was no longer pulling from after an earlier migration.
outcome: The verification step caught two more silent failures in the following quarter, both within a minute.
lesson: Verify the outcome, not the process. Green steps are a claim; the running build identifier is evidence.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known to treat every pipeline stage as a claim that needs independent confirmation.

title: A relief valve sized for the wrong scenario
problem: During a HAZOP revalidation we found a relief valve sized for fire case only, on a vessel whose worst case was blocked outlet.
context: Plant modified in 2015 to add a downstream pump. The relief study was never revisited after that change.
decision: We re-ran the full relief scenario set for the vessel rather than accepting the existing sizing basis.
reasoning: Relief sizing is only valid for the scenarios considered. A plant modification can introduce a new worst case that no one recalculated.
mistake: The 2015 modification was approved without triggering a relief system review, because the change looked small.
root_cause: The added pump made blocked outlet the governing scenario, requiring roughly twice the relief area installed.
outcome: The valve was replaced during the next turnaround, and modification approval now requires a relief review signature.
lesson: A small mechanical change can move the governing safety scenario. Tie relief review to the change process, not to a calendar.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known how often a modification quietly invalidates a safety study done years earlier.

title: A reporting pipeline that silently dropped a third of its rows
problem: Maintenance planning reports understated work orders by roughly 30% for two months before anyone noticed.
context: Nightly pipeline joining work orders to an asset table, with failures alerting only on job exit code.
decision: We added row count and join-match assertions between stages instead of only alerting on crashes.
reasoning: A pipeline that completes successfully can still be wrong. Correctness needs its own assertions, because exit codes only describe whether the code ran.
mistake: We monitored whether the job finished, and never whether the output was plausible.
root_cause: An inner join dropped work orders whose asset had been renamed, and renames had increased after a depot reorganisation.
outcome: The assertions caught two further data faults within a month, both on the same night they occurred.
lesson: Green pipelines are not correct pipelines. Assert row counts and join rates, and alert when they move.
what_i_wish_i_knew: I wish I had known that silent data loss is far more expensive than a loud crash.
